diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The trace does not establish a host or service fault that explains the reported slower coding task. python3 in the sole observed container had a short-lived CPU-use increase, but accounted CPU remained about 0.20 CPU-seconds per second for that process and 0.22 overall; the trace shows neither sustained CPU saturation nor a demonstrated scheduling, disk, or network bottleneck.
diagnosis.evidence: Used the recorded whole-trace range 03:17:26.200–03:17:59.000 and the workers' process-lifetime review; only pid_ns 4026531836 was substantial, with no clean service restart boundary. Compared the run_python sched_stat_runtime windows 03:17:26.200–03:17:41.200 and 03:17:41.200–03:17:56.200: python3 rose from 284.8 ms (19.0 ms/s) to 2,956.1 ms (197.1 ms/s), but all-process runtime in the latter window was 3,340.4 ms (222.7 ms/s), not evidence of host saturation. The workers also found no sustained wake-to-run delay, sampled block service times around 0.7–1.1 ms, and successful ordinary network sends. query_ctf returned unusable zero counts despite events being present, so those zeros were not treated as evidence. A check that could have falsified the no-fault conclusion is sustained CPU saturation or a persistent scheduling-delay increase during the python3 rise; the available runtime totals and raw scheduling samples do not show either. The recorded trace is short and cannot establish whether the task symptom occurred outside this interval.
diagnosis.window_evidence: No fault onset or recovery boundary is supported. The python3 CPU-use rise is visible by 03:17:41.200 and persists through 03:17:56.200, but its absolute rate and the observed kernel evidence do not establish that this was an incident; the late activity/count burst is at the trace end and was judged a possible drain, not a defensible onset.
